Dear Secretary Reese:

        Pursuant to sections 205 and 219 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”)1 and Part 35 of the
regulations of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or the “Commission”),2
Anchor Point Central, LLC (“Anchor Central”) respectfully requests that the Commission:

       1.      Approve Anchor Central’s transmission formula rate template (“Template”) and
               formula rate implementation protocols (“Protocols”, and together with the
               Template, the “Formula Rate”), to calculate Anchor Central’s net annual
               transmission revenue requirement (“ATRR”) for transmission investment in the
               Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”) region;
       2.      Authorize Anchor Central to use three incentive rate treatments: a regulatory asset
               incentive, a hypothetical capital structure incentive, and a regional transmission
               organization (“RTO”) participation incentive (together, “Incentives”); and
       3.      Authorize later-formed subsidiaries in MISO of Anchor Central’s parent company,
               Anchor Point Transmission, LLC (“Anchor Point Transmission”), to adopt the
               formula rate in connection with transmission projects in MISO (such affiliates, the
               “Anchor Point Transmission MISO Subsidiaries”).

      Anchor Central’s requests are just and reasonable. FERC has regularly granted such requests
for similarly situated new-entrant transmission development companies. The Template will
calculate Anchor Central’s ATRR, consistent with the MISO Open Access Transmission Tariff
(“MISO Tariff”). Consistent with Commission policy, the Incentives will provide a level playing

1
     16 U.S.C. §§ 824d, 824s (2024).
2

 field for Anchor Central to establish financial principles that incumbent transmission owners
currently have in place. Additionally, FERC’s authorization for Anchor Point Transmission to
adopt the formula rate for Anchor Point Transmission MISO Subsidiaries will conserve
Commission resources to the public benefit.

      Anchor Central respectfully submits that the Commission should approve the Formula Rate,
Incentives, and authorization for the Anchor Point Transmission MISO Subsidiaries to use the
same Formula Rate and Incentives (the “Filing”) as just and reasonable to facilitate urgently
needed transmission expansion under MISO’s competitive framework.

I.      INTRODUCTION

         Anchor Point Transmission is a new-entrant transmission development platform owned by
ArcLight Infrastructure Partners Fund VIII-A, L.P. (and its parallel funds) (together, “ArcLight
Fund VIII”) and managed by ArcLight Capital Partners, LLC (“ArcLight”). ArcLight is a leading
manager of infrastructure investment funds specialized in developing, managing, and operating
critical power infrastructure.3 ArcLight formed Anchor Point Transmission to (i) participate in
Commission-approved competitive solicitations to develop electric transmission, and (ii) partner
with electric utilities to solve transmission issues, optimize electric utility systems, and help
manage costs on these systems to the benefit of ratepayers. Anchor Point Transmission is focused
on the needs of small to mid-sized investor-owned utilities, municipal utilities, cooperatives, and
public power agencies.

        In accordance with the MISO Tariff and MISO’s governing documents, Anchor Central
will request that MISO file conforming changes to incorporate the Anchor Central Formula Rate
into the MISO Tariff at the appropriate time after the Formula Rate is accepted by the
Commission.4 Consistent with prior Commission approvals, Anchor Central submits its Filing
with an unpopulated formula rate and the Incentives in furtherance of leveling the playing field for
non-incumbent transmission developers and accelerating needed transmission investment.

II.   BACKGROUND

         Anchor Central is a non-incumbent transmission development company, focused on
transmission needs in the MISO region. Anchor Central plans to independently, and with partners,
pursue development opportunities in MISO’s Transmission Expansion Plan (“MTEP”), including
the Long-Range Transmission Plan (“LRTP”).5 With the support of ArcLight Fund VIII, Anchor
Central is expertly positioned to devote financial and operational resources to enhance the
reliability of the transmission system. Anchor Central is demonstrating this commitment by
actively working through the process to become a transmission-owning member of MISO. Though

        In the future, Anchor Point Transmission may create subsidiaries for certain transmission
projects in MISO. Thus, this filing includes a request to authorize such affiliates to use the same
Formula Rate and the same incentives for Anchor Central, as determined in this proceeding,
without re-litigation of hard-wired formula rate inputs.

        A. MISO’s MTEP and LRTP

        MISO undertakes a comprehensive regional transmission planning process through the
MTEP, including the LRTP. The MTEP is a fair and open regional planning process that considers
and evaluates projects for reliability, congestion relief, and public policy transmission needs.
MISO’s MTEP includes significant stakeholder participation, and the Commission deemed it
compliant with Order Nos. 890 and 1000.8 Approval of the Filing would further Anchor Central’s
participation in the LRTP.

         Under the MTEP, MISO, with stakeholder input, recommends certain regional and
interregional projects, including Market Efficiency Projects (“MEPs”) and Multi-Value Projects
(“MVPs”). MEPs and MVPs are subject to MISO Board of Directors approval. If approved, and
if the project is located in a state that does not mandate a right of first refusal for the incumbent
utility, MISO will undertake a competitive bidding process to select the developer to construct the
project. Under the LRTP, region-wide optimized transmission solutions could address reliability
issues more cost-effectively over the long term than incremental “bottom-up” upgrades developed
by individual transmission owners.9

III. SUMMARY OF REQUESTED ACTIONS

        A. Formula Rate

       Anchor Central requests that the Commission accept for filing its proposed forward-
looking Formula Rate, effective December 23, 2026. The Formula Rate will calculate Anchor
Central’s ATRR. The proposed Formula Rate is based on other formula rates accepted for filing

        B. Incentive Rate Treatments

       Anchor Central requests that the Commission authorize the following incentive rate
treatments:

        (1) Recovery of all prudently incurred pre-commercial, start-up and formation costs, and
            establishment of a regulatory asset including all expenses that are incurred prior to the
            time costs are first flowed through to customers under the MISO Tariff (“Regulatory
            Asset Incentive”);

        (2) Use of a hypothetical capital structure of 60% equity and 40% debt until Anchor
            Central first owns transmission assets that are placed in service and subject to MISO
            rates (“Hypothetical Capital Structure Incentive”), subject to a voluntary cap on equity
            of 60%; and

        (3) A 50 basis-point return on equity (“ROE”) adder to the base ROE (“RTO Participation
            Incentive”), conditioned on Anchor Central turning over functional control of all
            transmission assets it develops and owns to MISO.

        Anchor Central asks that the Commission approve the requested incentive rate treatments
by December 23, 2026 so that Anchor Central may (1) obtain regulatory certainty for application
of incentives to transmission projects that are approved under the MISO Tariff, in furtherance of
Anchor Central’s participation in MISO’s LRTP; and (2) credibly plan for partnerships with
electric utility partners, with the level of regulatory certainty required to access capital markets.

        C. Authorization for Anchor Point Transmission MISO Subsidiaries to Use the Same
           Formula Rate and Requested Incentives

      Anchor Point Transmission may create subsidiaries for certain transmission projects in
MISO. Accordingly, Anchor Central requests authorization for any Anchor Point Transmission
MISO Subsidiaries to use the same Formula Rate and the same requested incentives that are
approved for Anchor Central in this proceeding. Grounded in precedent, this prior approval would

IV.   CONTENTS OF FILING

       In addition to this letter, which provides a detailed description of the approvals requested
and the bases for those requests, this filing contains the following components:

V.    THE PROPOSED FORMULA RATE IS JUST AND REASONABLE

         Anchor Central requests that its proposed forward-looking Formula Rate be accepted for
filing effective December 23, 2026. Anchor Central proposes to use the Formula Rate to determine
the ATRRs for transmission projects in the MISO region as permitted by the LRTP under the
MISO Tariff. The Commission explicitly encourages the use of formula rates.12 Formula rates are

 the baseline standard for transmission-only utilities, providing cost transparency via the flow-

       As shown below, Anchor Central’s proposed Formula Rate, including the Template and
Protocols, is just and reasonable, consistent with FERC precedent.

        A. Formula Rate Design

        Anchor Central’s proposed forward-looking Formula Rate is similar to formula rates the
Commission has accepted for other competitive transmission developers in MISO.13 The Template
is the mechanism for calculating Anchor Central’s projected and actual net revenue requirements
in accordance with the procedures described in Anchor Central’s Protocols.14 The Protocols are
discussed in Section V.E below.

        The Template determines the ATRR based on operation and maintenance expenses,
administrative and general expense, depreciation expense, taxes other than income taxes, income
tax allowance, return on rate base, and any incentive rate adjustments, less any revenue credits and
agreed-to competitive adjustments for particular projects.

        Anchor Central is a pass-through entity for income tax purposes. Before revenues are first
collected under the Formula Rate and income taxes are first required to be recorded, a subset of
Anchor Central’s upstream parents will be classified, pursuant to an election under the Internal
Revenue Service’s entity-classification regulations, as entities taxable as corporations and subject
to corporate income tax. A portion of the income or losses from Anchor Central will be includable
on such parents’ income tax return, and such parents will be obligated to pay corporate income tax
on such amounts. Thus, Anchor Central will record income tax expenses and accumulated deferred
income taxes in its separate books of account even though a subset of its parents will pay these
taxes as costs-incurred.15 Accordingly, the Template provides for an income tax allowance that is
commensurate with the corporate income taxes that its parents actually incur in connection with
Anchor Central’s income or losses.16 This is consistent with Commission practice.17

        B. ROE

         C. Depreciation Rates

         As noted above, Anchor Central is a new entrant in the competitive transmission
development market, and it does not yet own transmission facilities. Thus, Anchor Central does
not have its own historical data on facility service life or net salvage estimates on which to support
a depreciation study. In similar circumstances where an applicant did not yet own transmission
facilities, the applicant has used, and the Commission has accepted, proxy depreciation rates based
on estimated service lives and net salvage rates developed for each depreciable group.20 As
explained by Mr. Allis, Anchor Central proposes to use representative depreciation rates (Exhibit
No. APC-402) for the electric transmission accounts developed from the expected function and
characteristics of the electric transmission facilities, information provided by Anchor Central, and
depreciation parameters used for similar transmission assets by other electric utilities. These proxy
depreciation rates would remain in effect until changed through an FPA section 205 filing based
on a future depreciation study of assets owned by Anchor Central or its affiliates within MISO, as
the Protocols provide, to analyze their life characteristics.21

         D. Competitive Project Adjustments

       The Template proposed by Anchor Central incorporates flexibility to make project-specific
competitive adjustments to the ATRR.22 Anchor Central may develop transmission projects for
which it has offered competitive adjustments for projects that, if accepted by MISO, would change
what could otherwise be collected under the Formula Rate as it relates to the awarded project. For
example, such adjustments could include concessions on project ROE or capital structure, or a cap
on project costs or revenue requirements. Anchor Central may also seek discrete incentive rate
treatments by separately filing for specific transmission projects that MISO awards to it. Any such
adjustments will be reflected, through lines 48 and 48a (page 3 of 5) of the Template, in the
determination of the ATRR, and Anchor Central will provide full documentation and support for
any competitive project adjustment made in the Annual Update process.

         E. Formula Rate Implementation Protocols

         Anchor Central witness Walter Hopkins describes the Protocols for populating the
Template and updating the ATRR calculation in his testimony.23 The Protocols are transparent,
consistent with the Commission’s guidance on protocols for forward-looking formula rates,24 and
will provide Anchor Central’s customers meaningful transparency, with procedural safeguards to
facilitate the annual review for assessment of the inputs to the ATRR.

       The proposed Formula Rate is forward-looking, determined based on projected accounting
values and then trued up after the relevant rate year based on actual accounting values. A forward-
looking formula rate as proposed herein is important to reduce lag between actual capital
expenditures and the recovery of such expenditures.

        The Protocols provide that, to calculate Anchor Central’s ATRR, Anchor Central forecasts
the values that populate the Template for each calendar year (Rate Year) and determines a true-up
of the forecasted values after the actual data becomes available on the FERC Form No. 1. Any
difference between the revenue collected and the actual ATRR for the relevant Rate Year will be
reflected in an appropriate true-up adjustment to the following year’s ATRR. Thus, for example,
Anchor Central would determine in 2029 (after submitting its FERC Form No. 1 covering 2028 in
April 2029) how the actual ATRR for 2028 differed from the revenue collected for 2028. Any
difference, along with interest calculated in accordance with section 35.19a of the Commission’s
regulations, will be reflected as a true-up adjustment to the forecasted 2030 ATRR. This ensures
that neither the customers nor Anchor Central are harmed if the forecasted ATRR differs from the
actual ATRR.25

        Anchor Central’s Protocols are consistent with the Commission’s instructions to other
entities with respect to (i) opportunities to participate in Anchor Central’s information exchange
process; (ii) the transparency of the information exchange; and (iii) the ability of interested parties
to challenge Anchor Central’s implementation of the Formula Rate.26 The Protocols establish a
transparent process governing the annual informational filing, information exchange between
Anchor Central and interested parties, and procedures for informal and formal challenges to
Anchor Central’s implementation of the Formula Rate.

         F. Authorization for Anchor Point Transmission MISO Subsidiaries to Adopt the
           Anchor Central Formula Rate

       Anchor Central requests that any later-formed Anchor Point Transmission MISO
Subsidiary be authorized to replicate, adopt, and implement the Formula Rate without the need to
rehash hard-wired inputs. Such approval would also permit the Anchor Point Transmission MISO
Subsidiary to submit a bid through the LRTP process that reflects the cost recovery it can expect,
which would provide greater accuracy in these estimates. The Commission has previously
accepted authority to replicate a single formula rate for use by multiple affiliated transmission
owners in the same region.27

        It would be administratively inefficient to require a new full-rate proceeding for an Anchor
Point Transmission MISO Subsidiary to pursue a new competitive bid project in MISO. The
Commission has repeatedly reasoned that this construct obviates the need to “re-litigate the
justness and reasonableness of a formula” where it is the same as the one first approved.28
Therefore, consistent with Commission precedent, Anchor Central respectfully requests
authorization for an Anchor Point Transmission MISO Subsidiary to replicate the Anchor Central
Formula Rate for future project companies in MISO.

VI.   ACCOUNTING

        Anchor Central witness Justin Campbell (Exhibit No. APC-100) provides an overview of
Anchor Central’s general accounting in support of the Anchor Central Formula Rate. Anchor
Central will utilize the accrual method of accounting as required by Generally Accepted
Accounting Principles to record revenues and costs, which will be recorded in accounts prescribed
by the Commission’s Uniform System of Accounts.29 As Mr. Campbell explains, Anchor Point
Transmission has established formal processes to review and approve all costs including costs
related to Anchor Central and such costs are reviewed periodically to track expenses and to monitor
charges to Anchor Central.30

VII. THE REQUESTED INCENTIVE RATE TREATMENTS ARE JUST AND
     REASONABLE AND WILL SUPPORT THE COMPETITIVE SOLICITATION
     PROCESS

        A. The Incentives Are Just and Reasonable.

       Consistent with FERC’s precedent concerning new entrant transmission developers
pursuing competitive transmission development opportunities, Anchor Central requests
authorization under section 205 of the FPA to utilize the Regulatory Asset Incentive and the
Hypothetical Capital Structure Incentive. The Commission has emphasized that such incentives

        Section 205(a) of the FPA provides for FERC to accept public utility rates that are just and
reasonable.32 The Commission has recognized its authority under section 205 of the FPA to
approve transmission incentive rate treatments “when they would promote the Commission’s
policies.”33 The Regulatory Asset and Hypothetical Capital Structure Incentives requested here
advance Commission goals on enhancing competition and leveling the playing field in
transmission development. Thus, the Commission should authorize use of the Regulatory Asset
and Hypothetical Capital Structure Incentives pursuant to its section 205 authority.

         The Commission has repeatedly approved the use of the Regulatory Asset Incentive and
the Hypothetical Capital Structure Incentive by new entrant competitive transmission developers,
finding that granting such incentive rate treatments under FPA section 205 advances the FERC
policy goal of establishing a more level playing field between incumbents and new entrants in
competition for new projects.34 The Commission has found that granting such incentives “will
facilitate the formation of additional entities for purposes of participating as nonincumbent
transmission developers in the Order No. 1000 transmission planning process, which is consistent
with our goals of removing barriers to transmission development and ensuring just and reasonable
rates through such processes.”35 It is just and reasonable to authorize the proposed Incentives to
level the playing field for Anchor Central to pursue competitive transmission opportunities for
projects consistent with the MISO Tariff and LRTP.

are first flowed through to customers under the MISO Tariff (Regulatory Asset Incentive).36

recovery.39 The Commission has found that the Regulatory Asset Incentive is an effective means
of encouraging transmission development by providing new entrant developers with upfront
certainty, reducing interest expenses, and improving coverage ratios. This incentive is needed so
that Anchor Central can record and recover formation, start-up and pre-commercial costs that were
not capitalized, but were incurred before such prudently incurred expenses could be recovered as
current expenses under the Formula Rate.40 The Regulatory Asset Incentive supports Anchor
Central’s status as a startup entity and Anchor Central’s ability to obtain financing on reasonable
terms and at a reasonable cost.

                 2. Hypothetical Capital Structure Incentive

        The Commission should grant the Hypothetical Capital Structure Incentive of 60% equity
and 40% debt until such time as Anchor Central first owns transmission assets that are placed in
service and subject to MISO rates. The Commission has found that a hypothetical capital structure
“can be an effective tool available to public utilities to foster transmission investment in
appropriate circumstances.”41 The Commission has allowed hypothetical capital structures for
transmission developers to facilitate “improved access to capital markets for transmission
investment and . . . for specific projects when shown to be necessary for project financing.”42

        Use of a hypothetical capital structure until such time as Anchor Central first owns
transmission assets that are placed in service and subject to MISO rates is appropriate to offset
risks and to improve Anchor Central’s access to capital. At first, Anchor Central intends to operate
with 100 percent capital infusions from its parent company. As construction on the first project
progresses, Anchor Central is expected to require additional capital contributions. As Mr.

37

is allowed for construction expenditures that accrue an allowance for funds used during construction. Grid Growth
Ohio, LLC, et al., 196 FERC ¶ 61,008, P 113 (2026). See 18 C.F.R. pt. 101, Electric Plant Instruction 3(17)(a).
38

regulatory asset balance beginning on the effective date of the Commission’s approval of this incentive until the
regulatory asset is included in rate base.

40

Commission has previously found that this incentive provides up-front regulatory certainty and can reduce interest
expense, improve coverage ratios, and assist in the construction of transmission projects.”) (citing DATC Mw.
Holdings, L.L.C., 139 FERC ¶ 61,224 (2012)); South Central MCN at P 26 (finding that a regulatory asset is just and
reasonable when applied to acquisitions of existing assets), order on reh’g, 154 FERC ¶ 61,271 (2016), order on
compliance, 161 FERC ¶ 61,053 (2017).

FERC ¶ 61,306, reh’g denied, 100 FERC ¶ 61,331 (2002), aff’d sub nom. Pub. Utils. Comm’n of Cal. v. FERC, 367
F.3d 925 (D.C. Cir 2004)).




                                                      - 11 -
 Campbell explains,43 the debt-to-equity ratio can be volatile as new debt and equity are invested.
Because of the initial reliance on capital contributions, which will persist even after Anchor Central
first owns transmission assets that are placed in service and subject to MISO rates, Anchor Central
will cap the equity portion of the cost of capital calculation to the lower of 60% or the equity
portion of Anchor Central’s actual capital structure. Anchor Central’s equity cap proposal is
consistent with past Commission orders involving requests from similarly situated startup entities;
in fact, two decades of precedent have allowed operating transmission companies to maintain
actual capital structures at this level.44

        As the Commission recognized in Tallgrass Transmission, LLC, use of a stable debt-to-
equity ratio for ratemaking purposes during construction provides certainty and improves access
to capital.45 In PATH, the Commission found that the use of a hypothetical capital structure during
construction “will result in lower debt costs for the company, while also permitting it to vary its
financing vehicles to the needs of the construction process, including such issues as timing of
expenditures, regulatory developments, and changes in financial market conditions.”46 It also
found the hypothetical capital structure approach during the construction period is a “pragmatic
approach to address . . . fluctuating capital structure” at the outset of a project’s development.47

        Furthermore, granting Anchor Central’s request for the Hypothetical Capital Structure
Incentive will help level the playing field with incumbents in competing for new projects.48 As the
Commission has repeatedly recognized, “nonincumbent transmission developers have a particular
need for the hypothetical capital structure incentive because it establishes certain financial
principles that incumbent transmission owners currently have in place but that remain
undetermined for nonincumbent transmission developers.”49 Accordingly, granting Anchor
Central’s request for a hypothetical capital structure will further the Commission’s policy of
leveling the playing field for nonincumbent developers, thus encouraging competition.

        Anchor Central’s requested Hypothetical Capital Structure Incentive would be in use only
until Anchor Central first owns transmission assets that are placed in service and subject to MISO
rates. At that point, Anchor Central would begin to use its actual capital structure subject to the
equity ratio cap at the lower of actual or 60%. Given the projected cost of a transmission project
and the resulting need for a material amount of investment during the construction phase, the use

        The Commission has approved the use of a hypothetical capital structure of 60% equity
and 40% debt for other new entrant transmission developers.50 The Hypothetical Capital Structure
Incentive requested is just and reasonable and appropriate to provide certainty, optimize the cost
of capital to the benefit of ratepayers, and promote the Commission’s policy of leveling the playing
field for nonincumbent developers seeking to participate in competitive developer selection
processes.

        The Commission has approved the use of the Regulatory Asset Incentive and the
Hypothetical Capital Structure Incentive for competitive developers, finding that these incentives
promote a more level playing field between incumbent and nonincumbent developers.51 The same
public policy objective of a level playing field is promoted by authorizing Anchor Central to utilize
these incentive rate treatments as it participates in the LRTP. Moreover, authorizing Anchor
Central to utilize the requested incentives will promote the Commission’s Order No. 1000 policy
of encouraging competitive transmission development as a means of putting downward pressure
on transmission development costs. In the context of competitive bidding, if Anchor Central has
knowledge of the incentive rate treatments available when pursuing competitive transmission
development opportunities, it will have a better basis for offering concessions from the full cost-
of-service rate in an attempt to win the project competition.

        B. The RTO Participation Incentive Is Just and Reasonable.

        Anchor Central requests a 50 basis-point adder to its base ROE in recognition of its
commitment to voluntarily turn over functional control of all transmission assets to MISO. The
Commission determined in Order No. 679 that it will approve ROE adders “for public utilities that
join and/or continue to be a member of an ISO, RTO, or other Commission-approved Transmission

 Organization.”52 As described above, Anchor Central is actively working to become a
transmission-owning member of MISO, will voluntarily transfer functional control of transmission
facilities it develops to MISO once they are put in service, and will recover the costs of its
transmission assets from MISO customers through the inclusion of its annual transmission revenue
requirement in MISO’s rates. The Commission has routinely approved the RTO Participation
Incentive for use by nonincumbent transmission developers that have not yet been awarded
competitive projects,53 and it should do the same here.54

         C. Approving the Use of the Requested Incentives by Anchor Point Transmission
            MISO Subsidiaries Is Just and Reasonable.

        Anchor Central seeks FERC authorization for Anchor Point Transmission MISO
Subsidiaries to use the requested incentives under the same terms and conditions proposed for
Anchor Central’s own use.55 This formulaic mechanism is both administratively efficient and
implemented here with transparency. FERC has approved such requests.56 Prior approval of these
incentives for Anchor Point Transmission MISO Subsidiaries will better enable these entities to
develop competitive bids with full information about their authorized rates.

       Authorization for Anchor Point Transmission MISO Subsidiaries to use the Regulatory
Asset Incentive, Hypothetical Capital Structure Incentive, and RTO Participation Incentive for
MISO transmission projects would be just and reasonable and should be granted for the same
reasons discussed in Sections VII.A and VII.B above.

VIII. PROPOSED EFFECTIVE DATE

       Anchor Central requests that the Commission accept the Formula Rate effective December
23, 2026. The Filing is consistent with Commission policy, as more fully supported by the
testimony and associated exhibits included as part of this filing. Further, Anchor Central is

 concurrently submitting an eTariff record for the purpose of ensuring a 60-day action date from

        Anchor Central requests that the requested incentive rate treatments be authorized as of the

       Anchor Central is making this filing at this time to obtain as much certainty as possible
about its authorized rate structure as a foundation for its development and submission of
competitive transmission bids in the MISO process. Acceptance of the Formula Rate and
authorization of the requested incentive rate treatments will help put Anchor Central on an equal
footing with incumbent transmission developers that already have formula transmission rates in
place.

IX.    REQUESTED WAIVERS

       Anchor Central respectfully requests waiver of the Commission’s Part 35 filing
requirements to the extent not satisfied by this filing. Anchor Central respectfully requests that the
Commission grant such waivers given the benefits of the proposed formula rate approach.

 50    Note D - Explanation of How ADIT Accounts are Remeasured Upon a Change in Income Tax Law
       Deferred tax assets and liabilities are adjusted (remeasured) for the effect of the changes in tax law (including tax rates) in the period that the change is enacted. Adjustments are recorded in the appropriate deferred tax balance sheet accounts (Accounts 190, 281, 282 and
       283) based on the nature of the temporary difference and the related classification requirements of the accounts. If as a result of action or expected action by a regulator, it is probable that the future increase or decrease in taxes payable due to the change in tax law or rates
       will be recovered from or returned to customers through future rates, a regulatory asset or liability is recognized in Account 182.3 (Other Regulatory Assets), or Account 254 (Other Regulatory Liabilities), as appropriate, for that probable future revenue or reduction in
       future revenue. Remeasurements of deferred tax balance sheet accounts may also result in remeasurements of tax-related regulatory assets or liabilities that had been recorded prior to the change in tax law. If it is not probable that the future increase or decrease in taxes
       payable due to the change in tax law or rates will be recovered from or returned to customers through future rates, tax expense is recognized in Account 410.2 (Provision for Deferred Income Taxes, Other Income or Deductions) or tax benefit is recognized in Account 411.2
       (Provision for Deferred Income Taxes-Credit, Other Income or Deductions), as appropriate.

 51    Note E - Computation of Excess or Deficient ADIT on Remeasurement Worksheets
       Each remeasurement summarized in the notes above (Note B, Note C, etc.) is computed on a corresponding remeasurement worksheet (Attachment 9b, etc.), which lists each temporary difference, the composite tax rates before and after the tax law change, and the resulting

25	Adjustment for Tax Law Changes with Prospective Effective Dates
In the case of tax law changes with an effective date(s) after the beginning of the test period, the impact of a timing difference on current tax expense or benefit differs from the impact on ADIT.  For example, in the case of a deductible timing difference originating in a tax year with a higher enacted tax rate than will apply when the difference will reverse, the current tax benefit will exceed the deferred tax expense.  In this situation, the adjustment computed below to recoverable income tax expense is made in order to avoid over-recovering income tax expense in the current test period due to the excess of current tax benefit over deferred tax expense (computed based on the estimated amount of the future tax liability) with respect to a given timing difference.  The adjustment to recoverable tax expense during the test period in which a timing difference originates mitigates the need for refund of a regulatory liability for excess deferred taxes in a future period (or, as applicable, the need for recovery of a regulatory asset for deficient deferred taxes in a future period).  Amounts in Column (37) are reported in the Income Tax Allowance Adjustment Mechanism - Summary on this worksheet.

50	Note D - Explanation of How ADIT Accounts are Remeasured Upon a Change in Income Tax Law
Deferred tax assets and liabilities are adjusted (remeasured) for the effect of the changes in tax law (including tax rates) in the period that the change is enacted.  Adjustments are recorded in the appropriate deferred tax balance sheet accounts (Accounts 190, 281, 282 and 283) based on the nature of the temporary difference and the related classification requirements of the accounts.   If as a result of action or expected action by a regulator, it is probable that the future increase or decrease in taxes payable due to the change in tax law or rates will be recovered from or returned to customers through future rates, a regulatory asset or liability is recognized in Account 182.3 (Other Regulatory Assets), or Account 254 (Other Regulatory Liabilities), as appropriate, for that probable future revenue or reduction in future revenue.  Remeasurements of deferred tax balance sheet accounts may also result in remeasurements of tax-related regulatory assets or liabilities that had been recorded prior to the change in tax law.  If it is not probable that the future increase or decrease in taxes payable due to the change in tax law or rates will be recovered from or returned to customers through future rates, tax expense is recognized in Account 410.2 (Provision for Deferred Income Taxes, Other Income or Deductions) or tax benefit is recognized in Account 411.2 (Provision for Deferred Income Taxes-Credit, Other Income or Deductions), as appropriate.										
											
51	Note E - Computation of Excess or Deficient ADIT on Remeasurement Worksheets
Each remeasurement summarized in the notes above (Note B, Note C, etc.) is computed on a corresponding remeasurement worksheet (Attachment 9b, etc.), which lists each temporary difference, the composite tax rates before and after the tax law change, and the resulting deficient (Account 182.3) or excess (Account 254) ADIT with tax gross-up.  The related deferred tax gross-up amounts are recorded in the appropriate ADIT accounts, as described in Note D.										
											
52	Note F - Accounting for Amortization of Excess or Deficient ADIT
The amortization of the deficient or excess ADIT reducing Account 254 (Other Regulatory Liabilities) is recorded with credits to Account 411.1 (Provision for Deferred Income Taxes – Credit, Utility Operating Income) and to Account 190 (Accumulated Deferred Income Taxes) or Account 283 (Accumulated Deferred Income Taxes—Other), as appropriate, in accordance with the Commission’s Accounting for Income Taxes Guidance.  The amortization of the deficient or excess ADIT reducing Account 182.3 (Other Regulatory Assets) is recorded with debits to Account 410.1 (Provision for Deferred Income Taxes, Utility Operating Income) and to Account 190 (Accumulated Deferred Income Taxes) or Account 283 (Accumulated Deferred Income Taxes—Other), as appropriate, in accordance with the Commission’s Accounting for Income Taxes Guidance.  This activity is summarized in the 'Amortization of Excess or Deficient ADIT' table (Lines 19a–24) of this attachment.  The annual amortization amounts are stated before tax gross-up; the gross-up to the revenue requirement level is applied in the Income Tax Allowance Adjustment Mechanism.

If projected and actual activity are both negative, a negative in Column (10) represents under-projection (i.e., the excess of actual activity over projected activity) and a positive in Column (10) represents over-projection (i.e., the amount of projected activity that did not occur).

H	Column (23) applies when (i) Column (21) indicates that ADIT activity was under-projected AND (ii) actual monthly and projected monthly activity are either both increases or both decreases.  Enter 50% of the amount from Column (21).  In other situations, enter zero.

ATTACHMENT C
Direct Testimony and Exhibits of
        Justin Campbell
                       UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                             BEFORE THE
               FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION



Anchor Point Central, LLC         )              Docket   No.   ER27-__-000




                            DIRECT TESTIMONY
                                    OF
                             JUSTIN CAMPBELL


                            ON BEHALF OF
                       ANCHOR POINT CENTRAL, LLC



                            EXHIBIT NO. APC-100




                              October 23, 2026
                                                                                                Docket No. ER27-___-000
                                                                                                   Exhibit No. APC-100
                                                                                                              Page i of i


                                              TABLE OF CONTENTS

I.      INTRODUCTION AND EXPERIENCE .............................................................. 1
II.     PURPOSE OF TESTIMONY ................................................................................ 4
III.    DESCRIPTION OF ANCHOR POINT TRANSMISSION .................................. 5
IV.     OVERVIEW OF THE APPLICATION ................................................................ 9
V.      OVERVIEW OF BUSINESS AND FINANCIAL RISK .................................... 11
VI.     DESCRIPTION OF ANCHOR CENTRAL’S ACCOUNTING ......................... 15
VII.    FORMULA RATE AND INCENTIVE PORTABILITY ................................... 17
VIII.   CONCLUSION .................................................................................................... 20
                                                                        Docket No. ER27-___-000
                                                                           Exhibit No. APC-100
                                                                                    Page 1 of 20



     I.   INTRODUCTION AND EXPERIENCE

 1   Q.   PLEASE STATE YOUR FULL NAME, TITLE, AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 2   A.   My name is Justin M. Campbell, IV. I am President of Anchor Point Transmission, LLC

 3        (Anchor Point Transmission), a dedicated transmission development platform owned by

 4        ArcLight Fund VIII (defined below) and managed by ArcLight Capital Partners, LLC

 5        (ArcLight). My business address is 222 W Las Colinas Blvd, Suite 1650E, Dallas, TX,

 6        75039.

 7   Q.   ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU TESTIFYING IN THIS PROCEEDING?

 8   A.   I am testifying on behalf of Anchor Point Central, LLC (Anchor Central), a wholly owned

 9        indirect subsidiary of Anchor Point Transmission.

10   Q.   PLEASE DESCRIBE YOUR PROFESSIONAL BACKGROUND.

11   A.   I am the President of Anchor Point Transmission, a newly formed non-incumbent portfolio

12        company of ArcLight. ArcLight hired me to assist with its transmission strategy and

13        identify new opportunities for ArcLight-managed funds to participate in the electric

14        transmission sector. The demand for capital and need for transmission development led to

15        ArcLight’s decision to found Anchor Point Transmission, a new transmission portfolio

16        company targeting opportunities to invest in the electric grid infrastructure. Since the

17        formation of Anchor Point Transmission, I have been focused on building a team of

18        transmission industry leaders to execute strategic partnerships and competitive

19        opportunities to develop, fund, own, and operate electric transmission. In my role as

20        President, I lead the company’s day-to-day activities and operations. I am ultimately
                                                                      Docket No. ER27-___-000
                                                                         Exhibit No. APC-100
                                                                                  Page 2 of 20


 1   responsible for identifying competitive transmission development opportunities and

 2   forming partnerships with utilities that can benefit from our expertise, experience, and

 3   capabilities. I oversee all regulatory work, community engagement, development, and

 4   execution to ensure deliverables are on schedule and cost-effective.

 5          Before I joined ArcLight, I was the Vice President, Power & Transmission at

 6   Tallgrass Energy. There, I led the company’s efforts to invest in efficient power facilities

 7   such as projects designed to convert waste heat to baseload, and carbon-free power. I also

 8   helped the company identify and advance opportunities to provide new sources of

 9   generation for computational loads.

10          Prior to joining Tallgrass, I served as Executive Vice President and Chief

11   Development Officer for GridLiance—a Blackstone portfolio company that has since

12   changed ownership. In that role, I led the growth of GridLiance’s portfolio of transmission

13   assets from pre-revenue startup through acquisitions and the development of several

14   successful partnerships with incumbent utilities. I also served as President of GridLiance

15   West LLC and President of GridLiance Heartland LLC. In that capacity I managed

16   GridLiance’s assets in the Western Interconnection and the Midwest, including its high-

17   voltage transmission lines under the operational control of the California Independent

18   System Operator (CAISO) and Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (MISO).

19          Before joining GridLiance, I served as Vice President of Edison Transmission,

20   LLC, an affiliate of Southern California Edison Co., which was formed to pursue new

21   growth opportunities nationwide. There, I helped develop the company’s competitive

22   strategy and led business development initiatives in various regional transmission
                                                                           Docket No. ER27-___-000
                                                                              Exhibit No. APC-100
                                                                                       Page 3 of 20


 1        organization (RTO) regions, including CAISO, MISO, PJM Interconnection L.L.C. (PJM),

 2        and Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (SPP). Prior to that, I held roles in Edison International’s

 3        strategic planning group and Southern California Edison’s Transmission & Distribution

 4        business unit.

 5               I began my career in the utility industry at the Federal Energy Regulatory

 6        Commission (FERC or the Commission) in 2003. At FERC, I worked on matters related

 7        to market-based rate sales of wholesale power and affiliate transaction rules. After leaving

 8        FERC, I worked for Houlihan Lokey, a global investment bank, where I managed complex

 9        financial analysis, including the valuation of public and private businesses for various

10        purposes.

11   Q.   PLEASE DESCRIBE YOUR EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND.

12   A.   I earned a Master of Business Administration from the University of Southern California

13        and a Bachelor of Science in economics and engineering science from Vanderbilt

14        University.

15   Q.   HAVE YOU TESTIFIED IN ANY FERC PROCEEDINGS?

16   A.   Yes. I testified in FERC Docket No. EC20-13, in which GridLiance Heartland LLC sought

17        authorization to acquire Electric Energy, Inc. and in FERC Docket No. ER19-191, in which

18        GridLiance West LLC sought authorization to recover its start-up regulatory asset. I have

19        also recently testified in FERC Docket No ER26-3696, in which Anchor Point Plains, LLC

20        filed its unpopulated formula rate template and protocols, and in FERC Docket No. ER27-

21        9, in which Anchor Point West, LLC filed its unpopulated formula rate template and

22        protocols.
                                                                            Docket No. ER27-___-000
                                                                               Exhibit No. APC-100
                                                                                        Page 4 of 20


     II.   PURPOSE OF TESTIMONY

 1   Q.    WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY?

 2   A.    The purpose of my testimony is as follows:

 3         •   To introduce Anchor Central, Anchor Point Transmission, and ArcLight;

 4         •   To provide an overview of this application and introduce the witnesses whose direct

 5             testimony will support Anchor Central’s application;

 6         •   To discuss the unique business and financial challenges faced by Anchor Central, as a

 7             new-entrant non-incumbent transmission developer in the MISO region;

 8         •   To describe Anchor Central’s accounting methodology and tax status;

 9         •   To support the request for authority for Anchor Point Transmission subsidiaries that

10             would directly own or develop specific transmission assets in MISO (Anchor Point

11             Transmission MISO Subsidiaries) to replicate Anchor Central’s Formula Rate

12             Template (Template) and Implementation Protocols (Protocols) (collectively, the

13             Formula Rate) and use the same incentive rate treatments that may be granted by the

14             Commission in this proceeding without relitigating those issues.

15   Q.    HAVE YOU PREPARED ANY EXHIBITS IN SUPPORT OF YOUR

16         TESTIMONY?

17   A.    Yes.

18             •   Exhibit No. APC-101 is an organizational chart illustrating the corporate structure

19                 of Anchor Central and its parent companies.
                                                                              Docket No. ER27-___-000
                                                                                 Exhibit No. APC-100
                                                                                          Page 5 of 20


     III.   DESCRIPTION OF ANCHOR POINT TRANSMISSION

 1   Q.     WHY WAS ANCHOR POINT TRANSMISSION FORMED?

 2   A.     Anchor Point Transmission was formed to identify and execute on strategic opportunities

 3          to build, fund, own, and operate electric transmission. We plan to (i) partner with utilities

 4          and communities to plan, build, own, and operate critical transmission infrastructure

 5          nationwide, and (ii) participate in Order No. 1000 and other regional transmission

 6          organization/independent system operator (RTO/ISO) competitive opportunities that align

 7          with ArcLight Fund VIII’s broader objectives to invest in assets critical to electrification

 8          and the digital economy. Anchor Point Transmission leverages its access to capital,

 9          industry expertise, regulatory experience, and execution capability to utilities and

10          communities facing growing reliability, load growth, and infrastructure needs. What

11          separates Anchor Point Transmission from its competitors is our ability to offer creative

12          and bespoke commercial structures to unlock grid investment in transmission. In an era of

13          unprecedented load growth, Anchor Point Transmission will serve a critical need by

14          leading the transmission buildout needed to meet our nation’s grid resiliency needs. Anchor

15          Point Transmission formed Anchor Central to partner with utilities, public power, and

16          electric cooperatives in MISO and to compete for Order No. 1000 competitive solicitations.

17          Together with its affiliated companies in other regions, Anchor Central is well positioned

18          to devote financial and other resources to enhance grid resiliency and reduce congestion to

19          the benefit of ratepayers, in part by providing tailored transmission solutions across the

20          MISO region.
                                                                           Docket No. ER27-___-000
                                                                              Exhibit No. APC-100
                                                                                       Page 6 of 20


 1   Q.   PLEASE PROVIDE AN OVERVIEW OF ANCHOR CENTRAL’S CORPORATE

 2        STRUCTURE.

 3   A.   Anchor Central is a Delaware limited liability company formed solely for the purpose of

 4        developing, constructing, owning, and operating transmission facilities in the MISO

 5        region. Anchor Central is a wholly owned indirect subsidiary of Anchor Point

 6        Transmission, which is a Delaware limited liability company. Anchor Point Transmission

 7        is a wholly owned direct subsidiary of Anchor Point Transmission Holdings, LLC (Anchor

 8        Point Holdings), which is also a Delaware limited liability company. Anchor Point

 9        Holdings is wholly owned, through subsidiaries, by ArcLight Infrastructure Partners Fund

10        VIII-A, L.P., ArcLight Infrastructure Partners Fund VIII-B, L.P., ArcLight Infrastructure

11        Partners Fund VIII-C, L.P., and ArcLight Infrastructure Partners Fund VIII-D, L.P.

12        (collectively, ArcLight Fund VIII).1 ArcLight serves as investment adviser to ArcLight

13        Fund VIII.

14   Q.   WHO OPERATES ANCHOR CENTRAL?

15   A.   Anchor Point Transmission is led by a senior team of utility professionals with decades of

16        experience in the transmission space. Initially, Anchor Point Transmission is leveraging its

17        deeply experienced team of executives employed by its affiliated management services

18        company, Anchor Point Management, in combination with external contractors to perform

19        operations and maintenance services and other essential start-up services. Over time, as

20        Anchor Central’s asset base grows, Anchor Point Transmission will scale up its team,



     1
          See Exhibit No. APC-101.
                                                                         Docket No. ER27-___-000
                                                                            Exhibit No. APC-100
                                                                                     Page 7 of 20


 1        increasingly performing these services with in-house personnel. Anchor Point

 2        Management has entered into a management services agreement pursuant to which it

 3        provides certain advisory, transactional, financial, management, consulting, development,

 4        operational and other related employee services to each Anchor Point subsidiary, including

 5        Anchor Central.

 6   Q.   DOES ANCHOR CENTRAL PRESENTLY OWN ANY TRANSMISSION

 7        ASSETS?

 8   A.   No. Anchor Central is a newly formed start-up transmission company and currently does

 9        not own or operate any transmission assets in MISO. However, Anchor Central is

10        demonstrating its commitment by actively working through the process to become a

11        transmission-owning member of MISO.

12   Q.   HOW IS ANCHOR CENTRAL PRESENTLY FINANCED AND HOW WILL

13        ANCHOR CENTRAL FINANCE ITS TRANSMISSION PROJECTS?

14   A.   Anchor Central is currently 100% funded through equity from the capital infusions of its

15        parent companies, Anchor Point Transmission and ArcLight Fund VIII. Because of its

16        newly formed start-up company status, Anchor Central does not have an established capital

17        structure. During the initial phases of development and construction of transmission

18        projects, Anchor Central will operate with capital infusions from its parent companies. As

19        construction of the projects progress, Anchor Central expects to obtain third-party

20        construction financing. Anchor Central’s debt-to-equity ratio is expected to fluctuate as

21        new debt and equity are invested. Anchor Central expects to obtain long-term debt at or
                                                                           Docket No. ER27-___-000

 8   Q.   CAN YOU PROVIDE ADDITIONAL DETAIL ON WHAT LENDERS WILL

 9        EXAMINE?

10   A.   When considering debt financing for a new project, lenders consider many different factors

11        to determine the project’s underlying credit strength and the appropriate size and level of

12        pricing. With electric transmission projects, there generally is not just one contributing

13        factor to credit strength. Rather, there is usually a combination of different attributes that,

14        when viewed together as a package, tends to underpin the overall credit quality of the

15        project. The attributes that contribute to successful financing include: (1) strong track

16        record and strong credit quality, and (2) a project that itself has an appropriate capital

17        structure, a durable regulatory compact and financial returns sufficient to attract the capital

18        needed to develop and construct the project. For a rate-regulated service such as

19        transmission, lenders will have an expectation that the project will maintain a fair

20        opportunity to earn a pre-established, reasonable ROE based on current capital conditions,

21        a specifically defined capital structure during development and construction, and

22        ultimately, the rate base and corresponding revenue streams on operation. Capital providers

 1        further expect that this framework is underpinned by an unequivocal authorization of the

 2        sponsor to construct the facility and to recover costs under the applicable tariff across

 3        diverse, creditworthy transmission customer bases.
